headline: Scientists Revive Ancient Proteins to Fight Modern Superbugs
meta_description: University of Oregon researchers reconstructed 160-million-year-old antimicrobial proteins that outperform modern human versions against drug-resistant bacteri…
summary_short: Scientists brought extinct antimicrobial proteins back to life—and some proved more powerful against superbugs than modern human versions.
body:
University of Oregon biologists have reconstructed antimicrobial proteins from extinct mammals that lived 160 million years ago, discovering that some ancient versions are more potent against antibiotic-resistant bacteria than modern human versions. The breakthrough, published in PLOS Biology in August 2026, offers a radically different approach to a growing medical crisis: as bacteria evolve resistance to antibiotics, nature's own ancient defenses may hold answers. The research traced the evolutionary history of lactoferrin, an immune protein found in breast milk, tears, saliva, and intestinal mucus, back to the earliest placental mammals near the end of the Jurassic Period. By comparing gene sequences from living species and using ancestral sequence reconstruction—a method pioneered at the University of Oregon—the team mapped how this protein changed over millions of years and recreated its prehistoric versions in the laboratory. Testing these resurrected peptides against pathogens including Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus revealed something striking: some ancient variants defeated drug-resistant bacteria more effectively than their modern counterparts.

The findings hinge on a surprisingly small detail. Researchers discovered that a single mutation in the protein's amino acid chain was enough to substantially boost the antimicrobial peptide's effectiveness. This suggests that evolution had already solved many of the design challenges that modern researchers are now struggling with—and those solutions are readable in the genetic record.

For biologists like senior author Matt Barber, the work reframes evolution itself as a resource. "Evolution is essentially a billions-year-old science experiment," he noted. By understanding what worked and what didn't in nature's long trial-and-error process, researchers can extract practical blueprints for designing new treatments. As antibiotic resistance grows more alarming each year, these ancient molecules offer not nostalgia, but genuine scientific hope.
